It prints exactly 4 lines, each "1" or "0", in this order:
  line1 = idna::is_valid_domain(input)
  line2 = idna::is_valid_label(input)
  line3 = idna::is_ascii_domain(input)
  line4 = idna::is_idn_domain(input)
With no argument, input defaults to the literal string "example.com".

- python3 / python are NOT installed. perl may not be installed.
- Use bash loops, printf, tr, head, sed, awk to build test strings.
- Handy helper you can paste:
    rep() { local n=$1 c=$2 s=""; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do s+="$c"; done; printf '%s' "$s"; }

- "" (empty)        -> 0 0 1 0
- "example.com"     -> 1 1 1 0
- "例子.测试"        -> 1 1 0 1

Be rigorous and quantitative. Bisect every boundary you claim (test N-1, N, N+1). Report exact reproducible command lines as evidence.

This is the single most important question — be exhaustive. - Test mixed ASCII+non-ASCII strings straddling the boundary.
- Test a string that is exactly 63 codepoints but 189 bytes, and one that is exactly 63 bytes but 21 codepoints — report line 2 for each. This disambiguates definitively.
- Report whether any Unicode normalization, case folding, or punycode conversion appears to happen (it likely does not — prove it).

  61*'a' + '\xE4\xBE\x8B' = 64 B -> 1 0 0 1
  60*'a' + '\xE4\xBE\x8B' = 63 B -> 1 1 0 1

rules.statement: NO Unicode normalization occurs (neither NFC nor NFD nor NFKC) before the length checks. Decomposed (NFD) u-umlaut = 'u' + U+0308 is 3 bytes/char and is measured as 3 bytes; the precomposed (NFC) U+00FC is 2 bytes/char and is measured as 2 bytes. The two forms therefore hit the 63-byte cutoff at different repeat counts.
rules.evidence:
NFD = 'u\xCC\x88' (3 B/cp)  vs  NFC = '\xC3\xBC' (2 B/cp), N repeats:
N=20  | NFD bytes=60 -> 1 1 0 1 | NFC bytes=40 -> 1 1 0 1
N=21  | NFD bytes=63 -> 1 1 0 1 | NFC bytes=42 -> 1 1 0 1
N=22  | NFD bytes=66 -> 1 0 0 1 | NFC bytes=44 -> 1 1 0 1   <-- DIVERGENCE
N=25  | NFD bytes=75 -> 1 0 0 1 | NFC bytes=50 -> 1 1 0 1
N=31  | NFD bytes=93 -> 1 0 0 1 | NFC bytes=62 -> 1 1 0 1
N=32  | NFD bytes=96 -> 1 0 0 1 | NFC bytes=64 -> 1 0 0 1
At N=22 the NFD string is 66 bytes and FAILS (line2=0); if NFC normalization were applied it would collapse to 44 bytes and PASS. It does not. Canonically-equivalent strings therefore give DIFFERENT answers.

rules.statement: NO NFKC / compatibility folding occurs. Fullwidth and compatibility characters that NFKC would map to ASCII remain non-ASCII: they report is_ascii_domain=0 / is_idn_domain=1 and keep their raw UTF-8 byte lengths.
rules.evidence:
$ ./test4_executable "ａｂｃ.ｃｏｍ"   # fullwidth 'abc.com', 19 bytes -> 1 1 0 1  (NOT 1 1 1 0)
$ ./test4_executable "ａ"              # U+FF41, 3 bytes         -> 1 1 0 1
$ ./test4_executable "１２３.com"       # fullwidth digits, 13 B  -> 1 1 0 1
$ ./test4_executable "ﬁ"               # U+FB01 ligature         -> 1 1 0 1
$ ./test4_executable "Ⅻ"               # U+216B roman numeral    -> 1 1 0 1

If NFKC ran, "ａｂｃ.ｃｏｍ" would become ASCII "abc.com" and line3/line4 would read 1 0.

rules.statement: NO case folding / case mapping occurs, and case never affects any of the four outputs. ASCII and non-ASCII uppercase/lowercase pairs give identical results, and no special-cased expansions (ß->ss, U+1E9B, U+0130) are applied.
rules.evidence:

$ ./test4_executable "ExAmPlE.cOm"  -> 1 1 1 0
$ ./test4_executable "Ü" -> 1 1 0 1   ;  $ ./test4_executable "ü" -> 1 1 0 1

$ ./test4_executable "İ"  -> 1 1 0 1   (U+0130)

rules.statement: NO punycode conversion happens in either direction. (a) Encoding: a 66-byte UTF-8 label whose punycode form would be roughly 40 ASCII chars (well under 63) still FAILS is_valid_label, so the length check runs on raw UTF-8 bytes, not on the A-label. (b) Decoding: already-punycoded input "xn--fsqu00a.xn--0zwm56d" (the A-label of 例子.测试) is treated as ordinary ASCII — is_ascii_domain=1 and is_idn_domain=0. There is no "xn--" prefix sniffing at all, in any case.
rules.evidence:

1
0        <-- fails on the 66 raw bytes; would pass if converted to punycode first

$ ./test4_executable "xn--"                     -> 1 1 1 0
$ ./test4_executable "XN--FSQU00A.COM"          -> 1 1 1 0
$ ./test4_executable "xn--a.com"                -> 1 1 1 0   (invalid punycode, still 1 1 1 0)

rules.statement: Neither is_valid_domain nor is_valid_label performs any structural parsing (no dot splitting, no per-label length enforcement, no leading/trailing-dot or empty-label rules) even with Unicode present. is_valid_label returns 1 for strings containing dots, and is_valid_domain returns 1 for a single 252-byte Unicode label that grossly violates the 63-byte per-label DNS rule.
rules.evidence:

$ ./test4_executable "例子.测试"     # 13 B -> 1 1 0 1
$ ./test4_executable "例."          # 4 B  -> 1 1 0 1
$ ./test4_executable ".例"          # 4 B  -> 1 1 0 1

rules.statement: Lines 3 and 4 (ascii/idn) are computed independently of validity and of length — they still report correctly on inputs that fail both validity predicates, including inputs far over 255 bytes. Execution is stable (exit code 0) on very large Unicode inputs up to at least 60,000 bytes.
rules.evidence:

$ ./test4_executable "$(rep 256 'a')"     # 256 B, invalid domain -> 0 0 1 0  (ascii still 1)
$ ./test4_executable "example.com$(printf '\xFF')" -> 1 1 0 1

N=1000  bytes=3000  -> 0 0 0 1 (rc=0)
N=5000  bytes=15000 -> 0 0 0 1 (rc=0)

rules.statement: Complete behavioral model for this dimension: let n = byte length of the raw argv string and hi = whether any byte >= 0x80. Then line1 = (1 <= n <= 255), line2 = (1 <= n <= 63), line3 = !hi, line4 = hi. Nothing else — no Unicode awareness whatsoever beyond the >= 0x80 byte test.
rules.evidence: This model was validated with zero mismatches on: (a) all 300 exact byte lengths 1..300 built from multi-byte-rich content, (b) 400 randomized mixed-alphabet strings, (c) all 255 single raw byte values 0x01..0xFF, (d) every targeted boundary case at 62/63/64/65 and 250..260 bytes across 4 different character widths and NFC/NFD forms. Combined outputs quoted in the rules above; the two sweep programs printed 'byte-length sweep 1..300 mismatches=0' and 'checked=400 mismatches=0'.

openQuestions: Embedded NUL (0x00) bytes cannot be passed through argv, so it is untestable whether the length predicates would use std::string::size() (counting the NUL) versus strlen semantics. Any C++ reimplementation should be aware this case is unobservable through this harness.

For the empty string, is_ascii_domain=1 and is_idn_domain=0 are consistent with both a vacuous 'no byte >= 0x80' quantifier and an explicit empty-string special case; the two are behaviorally indistinguishable here.
Exactly where argv size limits would start truncating is not probed beyond 60,000 bytes (all consistent with the model, rc=0). Behavior at multi-megabyte inputs / near ARG_MAX is untested.

Whether is_valid_domain and is_valid_label share one underlying length helper with different constants, or are two independent implementations, cannot be distinguished black-box — both are exactly consistent with a single byte-count comparison.
